topic: 450 XC-F 2017 weight, range, speed and engine feel
statement: A 2017 450 XC-F weighed 241 lb with a full 2.2-gallon tank and 230 lb without fuel, and listed at $10,099. It goes about 50 miles on a tank and runs into the limiter at 91 mph on stock gearing. The engine is torque-heavy and hooks up, and still revs freely on top. It stalls easily at small throttle openings if the clutch work is sloppy.

topic: 450 XC-F 2017 map switch and traction control
statement: The 2017 450 XC-F's bar switch gives four settings: two maps, each with traction control on or off, changeable while riding. The aggressive map suits good traction. The milder map with traction control on is easier when the throttle is opened fast, and traction control helps most for riders who spin the tyre or on loose ground.

On the 2017 450 XC-F the air fork has more small-bump compliance than the 2016 4CS. Testers added 1 psi and a few clicks of fork compression for balance, added up to five clicks of shock low-speed compression for the motocross track, and ran 103-108 mm of rider sag.

vals.fork: +1 psi, a few clicks more compression

statement: The 2017 450 XC-F has a close-ratio five-speed. Stock gearing tops out at 91 mph, and testers recommended re-gearing either way for tight trails or for fast desert, and wished for a sixth gear or wider spacing.

Findings on a 2017 450 XC-F: it stalls unless the idle is set properly; slipping the clutch heats the engine and the clutch damping rubbers should be checked every 20 hours; the exhaust is loud for off-road use; there is no skid plate and the handguards are light; the lithium battery needs warming before it cranks well in cold weather; and the push-button fuel cap is stiff when cold.

topic: 250 XC-F 2015 weight, range, speed and engine feel
statement: A 2015 250 XC-F weighed 247 lb with a full 2.4-gallon tank (about 15 lb less empty) and listed at $8,599. It went nearly 70 miles on a tank at a conservative trail pace, or about an hour at race pace, and ran 89-90 mph (98.1 with a tailwind). The power is long, smooth and linear and builds with revs to nearly 14,000 rpm. The flywheel effect is light, so stalls come suddenly.

The 2015 250 XC-F has the same engine and chassis as the 250 SX-F, with only a side-stand tab added to the frame. It adds a larger tank, the side stand, an 18-inch rear wheel, handguards and off-road suspension valving, on a six-speed semi-wide-ratio gearbox. The engine has a plain big-end bearing.

On the 2015 250 XC-F the 4CS fork's adjuster works mainly on mid-speed damping and needs 3-5 clicks before a change is felt, while 1-2 clicks on the shock are noticeable. For motocross, run it stock (riders under 165 lb may want softer springs). For off-road, go 3-5 clicks softer on fork compression and rebound, match the shock softer and take half a turn off the shock's high-speed compression. Sag is 100-105 mm. For tight racing add two rear teeth or drop one on the countershaft.

Findings on a 2015 250 XC-F: fork stiction on hard ground (oiling the seals and bleeding the air helped), a stock rear tyre that struggles on hard surfaces, fragile handguards that discolour, a touchy rear brake, no skid plate, and a loud muffler with no spark arrestor.

topic: TE 300 2019 fuel injection and oil injection
statement: The 2019 TE 300 is transfer-port injected: two injectors spray fuel into the transfer ports, and a 39 mm throttle body meters air and is where the auto-lube oil enters. The engine management reads six sensors (rollover, crankcase pressure, engine speed, throttle position, coolant temperature and intake air temperature). Oil comes from a 700 cc tank under the fuel tank at a ratio between 70:1 and 100:1, enough for four to seven tanks of fuel, with a low-oil warning light. It runs straight pump fuel of 91 octane or better and must use injector-compatible two-stroke oil.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Husqvarna TE300i race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2019 TE 300 made 49.77 hp at 8,600 rpm and revved to 9,600. The low-to-mid transition is slow, with a dip from 7,000 to 7,800 rpm on the stock map, then it climbs from about 43 hp to nearly 50 hp in under 1,500 rpm. The stock map (one mark) is the one to use; testers found the mellow map (two marks) poor.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Husqvarna TE300i race test

topic: TE 300 2019 tester settings on a motocross track
statement: A magazine crew's 2019 TE 300 setup for motocross. Fork (WP Xplor 48): compression all the way in (stock 15 clicks out), rebound 15 out, preload fully clockwise, legs flush. Shock: race sag 110 mm (stock 105), high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed compression 15 clicks out, rebound 15 out. Even at its stiffest the fork dives and the chassis oversteers under braking, and the ends are out of balance; racing it needs a revalve.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Husqvarna TE300i race test

topic: TE 300 2019 fixes for the slow midrange
statement: Tested answers to the 2019 TE 300's slow low-to-mid power: a 51-tooth rear sprocket in place of the stock 50 (13/50 is the US gearing), holes drilled in the airbox, the stock map, the optional quick-turn throttle cam, and an aftermarket pipe, which filled the 7,000 rpm dip.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Husqvarna TE300i race test

statement: The oil tank on the 2018 injected TE 300 could leak. Testers reported it fixed for 2019.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Husqvarna TE300i race test

statement: On a rear-wheel dyno the 2019 injected TE 250 made 40.74 hp at 8,230 rpm and 27.49 lb-ft at 7,580 rpm. It is a 249 cc engine (66.4 x 72.0 mm, 13.2:1) with transfer-port injection, and holds low rpm well in second gear. List price $9,699.

source.name: Dirt Rider - 2019 Husqvarna TE 250i dyno test

statement: Of the 2016 two-strokes, the TE 250 is the livelier, with smooth, predictable power, less vibration and a lighter feel. The TE 300 pulls harder from the bottom and needs less clutch in slow going. Both feel planted and are less likely to deflect off roots and rocks than the 125. Both have a two-map switch on the bar.

topic: FE 350, FE 450 and FE 501 ride character (2016)
statement: Of the 2016 FE four-strokes, the 350 is very usable and can be revved or lugged, though its weight shows when changing direction or slowing. The 450 has strong, usable power and finds traction well in tight going, with suspension that works best when pushed, but it is a lot of bike for a full day. The 501 is extremely powerful and limited by grip off-road: it is best left in third gear with a finger on the clutch, feels heavy in tight terrain, and an auto-clutch was suggested for it.

The street-legal 2016 FE 501 weighs 250 lb without fuel, holds 2.4 gallons and listed at $10,599. It has a heavier crankshaft than the off-road FE 501, 11.8:1 compression, a 42 mm throttle body and a quiet exhaust, with tall road gearing (first is good for over 30 mph). It has tractable torque at any speed and the suspension takes hard hits well. The front end feels light with no steering damper, the stock rims are unbalanced and bounce at highway speed, the tank is small for long rides and no handguards are fitted.
notes: Source tested the street-legal S version.

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling - 2016 Husqvarna FE 501 S test

statement: On the 2017 TE 250 and TE 300 the stock suspension is soft and at times short of control for a rider over about 90 kg. Gearing felt tall for tight going; two or three more teeth on the rear were suggested. The 300 is strong, linear and nearly vibration-free but snappy in the upper midrange when the rider is tired, and the 250 is more controllable and less tiring. Three power-valve springs are supplied for tuning the hit. Dry weights are 102.2 kg (250) and 102.4 kg (300).

vals.gearing: +2 or 3 rear teeth for tight terrain

source.name: BikeReview - 2017 Husqvarna TE 250 and TE 300 review

statement: In competition tune a 2018 FE 350 made 48 PS at 10,000 rpm and 39.7 Nm at 7,900 rpm on a magazine dyno, and weighed 114 kg with a full 8.5-litre tank. The bar switch changes throttle response between two settings and traction control can be switched on or off. The suspension responds well over bumps and has reserve for big jumps.

In 2019 the FX 350 is a hybrid of motocross and enduro parts: about 6 kg lighter than the FE 350, with the WP AER 48 air fork and the 2019 motocross-range engine and chassis upgrades the FE did not yet have. The FE 350 has a sharp-steering chassis with forgiving power and suspension that suit tight, slippery terrain.

The 2016 450 XC-F took the new, smaller and lighter chassis and engine at the same time as the 450 SX-F and performs identically on power: smooth, torquey, able to chug at low revs and pull away on the throttle. Its off-road valving has less high-speed compression and rebound damping than the SX-F, so it is plusher without wallowing, the 4CS fork is less harsh at the top of the stroke than earlier versions, and it still copes with a motocross track. A rubber-mounted bar cuts vibration. It is a lot of bike in tight woods, resists turning more than the 350 XC-F, and suits open terrain, desert and GP-style racing.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test - 2016 KTM 450XC-F riding impression

statement: The 2016 XC-F models share frame, engine and mapping with the SX-F motocross bikes and add an 18-inch rear wheel, handguards, off-road suspension settings, a 2.25-gallon tank (1.85 on the SX-F) and a side stand. The 250 XC-F gained torque and bottom-end with a smoother move into the midrange and is strong on tight, technical ground. The 350 XC-F has a wide powerband with a strong bottom but needs more shifting on a track. The 450 XC-F has heavy bottom-end torque and is best ridden a gear higher than usual; ridden like a motocross bike it wears the rider out.

source.name: Cycle News - 2016 KTM SX-F and XC-F first rides

statement: For 2013 the 500 XC-W got new fork oil for more consistent damping, a rear brake master cylinder with less seal wear, and black-coated spokes on new rims. It is a 510.4 cc (95 x 72 mm) four-stroke with a hydraulic clutch, a 48 mm WP open-cartridge fork (300 mm travel) and a PDS shock (335 mm), 13/50 gearing, a 2.25-gallon tank and a 970 mm seat, and weighs about 247 lb without fuel. US list price $9,649.
For 2015 the 500 XC-W got a lighter DDS clutch basket and new O-rings on the oil-pump suction screen for durability.

source.name: Off-Road.com - 2015 KTM dual-sport and cross-country bikes

topic: FX 350 and FX 450 2019 engine and chassis changes
statement: For 2019 the FX 350 and FX 450 got a stiffer frame and triple clamps, a two-piece subframe about 9 oz lighter, new damping in the AER 48 fork and a shock with a new main piston, radiators mounted nearly half an inch lower, slimmer bodywork, new header pipes with a resonance chamber that come off without disturbing the shock, a shorter muffler, new launch and traction control settings and skid-plate mounts. The FX 450 got a lower cylinder head nearly 18 oz lighter with a new camshaft. The FX 350 got a head 7 oz lighter, larger titanium valves and a diaphragm-spring steel clutch that saves nearly 7 oz; it revs to 13,400 rpm.

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling - 2019 Husqvarna cross country line-up first look

topic: FX 350 2018 map switch, traction control and launch control
statement: The 2018 FX 350's bar switch chooses between two maps, turns traction control on or off and arms launch control for starts. Traction control compares throttle position with how fast the revs are rising and trims power when they climb too quickly. The bike is a 349.7 cc DOHC six-speed (semi-close ratios) with a Magura hydraulic clutch, the WP AER 48 fork (310 mm travel), a linkage shock (300 mm), a 2.25-gallon tank and a 960 mm seat, and weighs 221.8 lb without fuel.

A magazine crew ranked the 2013 450 SX-F second of six: 56.95 hp at 9,400 rpm and 240 lb, with the most power over the broadest range and the best brakes, clutch, handling, shifting and starting. The stock WP fork and shock were its weak point and the shock preload ring does not hold a true setting.

A magazine crew ranked the redesigned 2013 CRF450R fourth of six: 51.55 hp at 8,900 rpm, the lowest in the test, at 234 lb. It was the easiest bike to use, with handling and clutch improved over the 2009-2012 bikes, but the power falls off early and is flat by 8,200 rpm.

A magazine crew ranked the 2013 YZ450F fifth of six: 55.24 hp at 9,100 rpm and 238 lb, with the top-rated fork and shock and very good durability. The powerband is disjointed, turn-in is flawed, the radiator wings are wide and the airbox is noisy.

A magazine crew ranked the 2012 450 SX-F second of six at 243 lb: electric start, a self-adjusting hydraulic clutch with the new diaphragm spring, smooth carburetted delivery and strong brakes. The bars are low, the shock preload ring is weak and the fuel cap is hard to use.

A magazine crew ranked the 2012 CRF450R fifth of six: the lightest at 231 lb, with comfortable ergonomics and a steering damper, but several horsepower down on its rivals with a flat top end, a four-spring clutch they rated nearly useless, a twitchy front end in rough sections and gearing that is too tall.
A magazine crew ranked the 2012 350 SX-F last of six in their 450-class shootout, where it was measured against full 450s.

A magazine crew ranked the 2011 450 SX-F first of six: the broadest, easiest powerband, the best clutch, standout brakes, neutral handling and electric start. The understeer of earlier chassis was gone and they listed no significant flaws.

A magazine crew ranked the 2011 YZ450F third of six: the best suspension and shifting and strong reliability, a safe choice, but with an engine they called acceptable and no more, on a bike virtually unchanged from 2010.

A magazine crew ranked the 2011 350 SX-F fifth of six against 450s. Its handling was rated very, very good, but it is sluggish until about 9,000 rpm, peaks at 12,200 rpm, gives away about 10 hp to a 450 in the midrange and is only five pounds lighter than the 450 SX-F. The suspension is too soft: they recommended the 450 SX-F's fork and shock.

A magazine crew ranked the 2011 CRF450R last of six: light, with a pleasant, mellow powerband, but a clutch they rated useless, handling that oversteers and wanders, and suspension that is stiff at the rear and soft at the front.

A magazine crew ranked the 2012 CRF250R fourth of five: 38.44 hp at 11,000 rpm, 222 lb, $7,420, with a strong midrange and a new linkage that settles the rear. The frame geometry brings oversteer and headshake, the forks dive under braking, the springs are too soft for riders over 165 lb and the exhaust holds back the top end.

A magazine crew ranked the 2012 YZ250F third of five: 37.13 hp at 11,500 rpm, 218 lb and $7,250, with the best suspension in the class, first for durability and a stable, forgiving chassis. The engine is a low-to-mid design and the only carburetted one in the class; they called it sluggish.

A magazine crew ranked the 2012 250 SX-F last of five: 35.52 hp at 10,800 rpm, the lowest, at 231 lb, the heaviest, and $7,699. It had the best brakes and clutch and handles precisely once set up. To fix the harsh fork and odd spring rates they raised the shock spring from 5.1 to 5.4 kg/mm and drained some fork oil.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 YZ250F first of six: coil-spring suspension, a versatile engine, strong all-round handling and durability. It has the weakest front brake in the class, feels loose in flat turns and testers swapped the stock bar bend.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 KX250F second of six on the broadest usable power in the class. It understeers and the shock wallows in corners (different offset clamps and a longer link arm), it resists shifting under load and the clutch does not last like the hydraulic ones (stiffer springs). Use the white coupler.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 CRF250R third of six: good air forks once set, comfortable ergonomics and a progressive front brake, but about 5 hp down on the class leaders, nervous at high speed and with a soft, fading clutch. Setup: 105 mm of sag with the forks lowered in the clamps; heavier riders 100 mm and a quarter turn more high-speed compression.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 FC 250 fifth of six despite more than 43 hp, a hydraulic clutch, a strong front brake and a two-position map switch. The airbox dulls throttle response, the suspension stays stiff and the power is all on top. Their fixes: drain 10 cc from each fork leg, drill the airbox cover (and clean the filter more often), raise the fork legs 15 mm and run 105 mm of sag.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 250 SX-F last of six: it has a hydraulic clutch, the best front brake, electric start and reliability, but poor drive out of corners, a powerband too high in the revs and forks too stiff to move. Use fork height to balance the chassis and lower the fork oil 10 cc if it feels harsh.

A magazine crew ranked the new 2019 YZ250F first: an easy, usable powerband, coil-spring suspension that is plush early and resists bottoming, and a durable build. At 228 lb it is heavy, feels it at turn-in and is the widest bike in the class. The free phone app changes the maps.

In a magazine's 2019 250 shootout the 250 SX-F made the most power, 42.65 hp at 13,800 rpm, and was the lightest at 219 lb, with the best brakes, clutch, shifting and front-end grip. Its power is mellower than 2018, the chassis and suspension are stiffer and the airbox is restricted; it suits fast riders better than average ones.

In a magazine's 2019 250 shootout the FC 250 made 42.53 hp at 219 lb and $9,099, the dearest in the class. The plastic airbox is restrictive and it lost power against the 2016 engine: drill the airbox cover. Perforating the muffler's backfire screen also helps but the screen may then burn through.

In a magazine's 2019 250 shootout the CRF250R made 42.40 hp at peak but was down as much as 4 hp from 7,000 to 10,000 rpm, so it is sluggish low to mid, hard on clutches and at its worst on tight tracks. The chassis and suspension are plush and comfortable; the fork is soft and can bottom for heavy or fast riders.

A magazine crew ranked the 2019 KX250 fifth: the best bottom-end in the class, slim, precise and the most adjustable, at $7,749, the cheapest. The top end is flat, the clutch wears (heavier springs or a complete aftermarket clutch), the fork is harsh mid-stroke as on the 2018, and there is no electric start.

The 2018 FC 350 and 350 SX-F both make 54 hp at 13,400 rpm and share forks and shock. The Husqvarna differs in its sealed plastic airbox with no vents, composite subframe, a baffled muffler, Magura clutch hydraulics (Brembo on the KTM), different bars, rims and brake discs, and a seat that is longer, thinner and 5 mm lower with about half the foam. It is two pounds heavier. Its low-end is muted and its delivery steadier and more metered; testers found it plusher and better handling, and some veterans preferred it in ruts and off-cambers.

topic: FC 350 2018: making it run like the KTM
statement: Tester fixes for the 2018 FC 350: cut away part of the right side of the airbox and drill the left cover; replace the baffled muffler with the unrestricted FC 250 muffler or a slip-on; fit the other Austrian brand's slave piston and O-ring to cure the clutch slave seal failures; thread-lock the rear sprocket bolts and check the spokes beside the rim lock before each moto. Husqvarna riders often gear down two teeth at the rear.

In a magazine comparison the 2018 350 SX-F beat the FC 350: 54 hp at 13,400 rpm with snappier throttle response from its vented airbox and straight-through muffler, two pounds lighter, and without the Husqvarna's clutch slave seal risk. It took the power, brakes and clutch categories; the Husqvarna took handling and wheels. KTM racers typically add one tooth at the rear. Thread-lock the sprocket bolts and check the spokes next to the rim lock before each moto.

A magazine crew narrowly ranked the 2015 YZ250 first of three 250 two-strokes on the balance of suspension, power delivery, comfort and reliability, even though it was the weakest on the dyno, the slowest off the line and had the weakest brakes. Stock jetting runs clean on pump fuel and changes tend to make it lean. Raising the fork in the clamps with about 107 mm of sag helped cornering at the cost of high-speed stability. The clutch needed frequent adjustment.

In a magazine's 2015 250 two-stroke shootout the 250 SX had the strongest dyno numbers, peaking at 8,400 rpm, and the best holeshot, with a strong hydraulic clutch and brakes. The power drops quickly after the peak, so it is short-shifted, it vibrates the most, it ran rough on 91-octane pump fuel until rejetted, and the fork and shock are hard to balance.

In a magazine's 2015 250 two-stroke shootout the TC 250 cornered best of the three, with a smooth powerband from its sealed airbox, but it lacks the KTM's midrange punch, the suspension is hard to balance and riders were less confident on big jumps. The aggressive map (setting two) worked best. Against the 250 SX it has wider, curved bars, a slipperier seat and less vibration.
